claim.pdf_says: Flowchart (Figure D.10): condition-1 true 'yes' and condition-2 false 'yes' both lead to 'Evaluate condition-3'; condition-2 false 'no', condition-3 false 'yes' and condition-4 false 'yes' lead to 'Truth value is false'; condition-4 false 'no' leads to 'Truth value is true'.
claim.why_it_matters: Flowchart flattened to labels; the markdown juxtaposes 'no' with 'Evaluate condition-3', although in the figure condition-2's 'no' leads to 'false' and its 'yes' leads to condition-3, so the flattening reads backwards.

verdict.reasoning: Rendered PDF page 893 (printed p.869) shows Figure D.10. The claim describes its edges correctly: c1 yes and c2 yes go to Evaluate condition-3; c2 no, c3 yes and c4 yes go to 'Truth value is false'; c4 no goes to 'true'. The markdown keeps every label and box text (Evaluate condition-1..4, Condition-1 true, Condition-2 false, Condition-3 false, Condition-4 false, every yes/no, both truth-value terminals) in top-to-bottom reading order, and it keeps the caption verbatim, which states the expression the chart evaluates: (condition-1 OR NOT condition-2) AND condition-3 AND condition-4. The 'no Evaluate condition-3' run is not misquoted text. The 'no' under Condition-2 and the 'Evaluate condition-3' box sit at the same height on the page, so the flattening puts them on one line. The connecting lines are lost, as they are in every flowchart flattened to text. That is a layout artifact of an informative Annex D figure, not a changed or missing label, and the caption fully determines the semantics. A reader cannot take the flattened text as an assertion that 'no' leads to condition-3. No genuine content discrepancy.
